texts.CO: The course Bio-organic Chemistry for Life Sciences gives a conveniently arranged introduction in bio-organic chemistry, with a focus on natural products / bio-molecules. Structure and reactivity of molecules, reaction mechanisms, stereochemistry, and interactions between molecules form the backbone of this course. It forms a solid basis for further studies in life sciences. The course is composed of lectures, tutorials and a practical part. The course is taught in Dutch in period 1 and in the afternoon of period 4. It is taught in English in the morning of period 4.
texts.AC: Students must study the reader following the presented study guide. In the lectures the basic concepts are explained. Audio-slides are used to prepare for tutorials. During the tutorials questions from the workbook are exercised and discussed with the teacher. Students can exercise online assignments as a self-check. In the practical part, which is closely related to the theoretical part, different basic laboratory skills are exercised, like extraction and chromatography, making use of natural products (lipids, carbohydrates, and peptides). To work safely and concern for the environment are important aspects in this part.
texts.LT: Reader ORC13803 and workbook ORC13803.

texts.CO: The Ecology course provides an introduction to and overview of the field of ecology, thereby creating a foundation for various advanced courses in the years to come. It builds on the material you learned in your pre-university/secondary school courses in biology. In the course you will become conversant with the most important theories and principles of general ecology based on interesting examples from scientific research and the practice of nature management, agriculture and fisheries, land development and environmental policy. Ecological insights are essential for solving major problems concerning biodiversity, food production, global climate change and many other areas.
texts.AC: Ecological principles are studied from a handbook supported by a course reader. Relevant chapters are introduced in oral lectures. Specific subjects are studied in intensive tutorials  under supervision of a lecturer. Field aspects of ecology are demonstrated in field practicals highlighting typical environmental and landscape characteristics and nature management of the Veluwezoom and Rhine valley near Wageningen. Participation in intensive tutorials  and the field practicals is obligatory.

texts.CO: This course is complementary to and runs parallel to Ecology I (PEN10503) and serves to train students in practical investigations of ecological issues and problems. Ecology-2 is specifically set up for first year Bachelor students in Biology and Forest and Nature Conservation and Plant Sciences. The course is given during the 1st and 6th period of the first year. The aim is to learn and understand ecological concepts by performing data-yielding experiments under field, greenhouse and/or laboratory conditions (practical part) and writing a short literature-based project proposal targeting a current ecological problem (project part). The students report their results by means of writing two reports, one for the practical part and one for the project part, as well as a presentation for the project part.
texts.AC: (1) Field and laboratory practicals are carried out in small (2-3 students) groups under the skilled supervision of teaching staff. Dealing with ecological themes like biodiversity, variation in ecosystems, climate and ecosystems, agroecology, life cycles and population dynamics, students identify project aims, collect data, conduct basic data analyses, and report on these, both in writing and orally. The added value here is to solve an ecological problem by means of group activity under supervision of a teacher. (2) Within the broad setting of ecology, small (ca 5 students) groups each narrow down on a group-specific research question under the skilled supervision of teaching staff. Searching for peer-reviewed and other scientific papers, students write a project proposal with proper scientific framing and phrasing, leading to academic and practical conclusions, backed-up with references. Students present this proposal in a written and an oral form.

texts.RES: Reports that were graded insufficient can be re-submitted in the resit period. For those that did not reach the limit of attendance (max 1 missed meeting in both the practical and the project part), they need to repeat the respective part of the course in the following academic year.

texts.CO: This course is part of the first year program for Biology, Biotechnology, Molecular Life Sciences, Nutrition and Health and Plant Sciences students. The course content provides necessary knowledge for continuation courses in all these study programs. Cell Biology forms an introductory and partly specialized course into the structure and function of plant, animal and bacterial cells and biomolecules.   Special focus is directed at the ultrastructure and function of the different cell organelles, the cytoskeleton and cellular organization. Furthermore, the molecular and biochemical basis of cell function and cell differentiation processes are discussed. Recent research insights into cellular mechanisms are applied in the course. Basic principles of intra- and extracellular communication processes will be studied to obtain insight into the regulation of cell function in the context of whole tissues, organs and complete organisms. Every week has a theme and in relation to this theme there will be a practical and a group discussion. During practicals students explore, among others, mitosis and meiosis in plant and animal cells, transcriptional regulation in bacteria and the role of membranes in cell homeostasis (e.g. vacuoles, cholesterol, receptors, channels and transporters). Additionally, there is a case integrating the topics of that weeks, such as pharmaceutical compounds of plants, role of neurotransmitters in depression and regulation of cell cycles.
texts.AC: Every week is started with a new theme.This is introduced during plenary lectures. Theory is supported by ICT modules. Subsequently students work in small groups of 12 students wherein they are offered case studies with specific tasks that have to be prepared during the week and presented in mandatory group discussions at the end of each week. Cases should challenge the students to analyse the related subjects in the light of the weekly theme. If a mandatory group meeting is missed due to valid reason a replacing assignment can be requested by the course coordinator. The weekly learning goals comprise the knowledge needed to understand and explain the case. Laboratory practicals are a mandatory part of the course. The biological assays  chosen are related to the weekly theme as well as the cases under study. Techniques applied are microscopy and cell biological analyses, supported by computer modules and short movies. Practical reports provide basic skills in scientific writing.

ISBN 978-1-324-03339-4 A Brightspace environment is available with specific literature, ICT modules, movies and PowerPoint presentations of the lectures.

texts.AK: Chemistry at Dutch VWO level or comparable.
texts.CO: Living organisms have a remarkable capacity to regulate physiologically the inner environment. Electrolyte levels, pH-levels, redox potentials are all kept within certain limits to ensure internal stability. Several organs including the liver, the kidneys, and the nervous and endocrine systems help maintain homeostasis by triggering biochemical and physical-chemical mechanisms. In this course we will focus on the general chemical or (physical-chemical) mechanisms on a molecular level that are involved in the Life Sciences. These mechanisms include energy exchange, Gibbs free energy as driving force, molecular interactions, various types of equilibrium, buffer systems, ATP-coupling and reaction kinetics. Some of these mechanisms are interpreted from the first and second laws of thermodynamics.

texts.CO: All living organisms have evolved and continue to do so. Evolutionary biology studies the history of that process and the mechanisms that cause it to happen. This introductory course treats microevolution (the evolutionary changes occurring within populations and species over a limited number of generations), organismal design by selection for reproductive success, and macroevolution (the evolution of new species and the long-term evolutionary changes above the species level). It distinguishes between the two general methodologies to study evolution: the direct experimental study of processes (often using microbes in the laboratory) and the comparative method that interprets relatedness patterns among now-living organisms to test hypotheses. These are the specific themes and subthemes that will be treated: microevolutionary concepts, population genetics, design by selection for reproductive success, principles of macroevolution, the history of life, integrating micro- and macroevolution.
texts.AC: In total (parts of) 16 chapters of the book "Evolutionary analysis" by Herron & Freeman will be studied. For each chapter the following activities are planned: First, the student reads reading guide and chapter and performs a short quiz (self test).    Next day, one or two lectures about the chapter will focus on the essential concepts and will provide illustrations, as well as information required for the tutorials.   - After the lectures the student will work in pairs on assignments during supervised tutorials or practicals. - Additional learning activities include watching a movie introducing Darwin's ideas, the collection of your own ancestral data, an excursion to Naturalis with "field-work assignment", and weekly lunch discussion meetings on topics of choice.

texts.CO: The Zoology course centers on understanding the phenotype of vertebrates, emphasizing the continual adaptations animals make to thrive in their environments. You'll learn how the morphology (form) of tissues, organs, and even entire organisms is closely tied to their functions. We begin with the relationship between ontogeny (embryonic development) and phylogeny (evolutionary history), using the EVO-DEVO model. This framework enables us to explore the fundamental ancestral blueprint (bauplan) of vertebrates, such as the shark, alongside the specialized adaptations required for diverse lifestyles.  The course then progresses to examine structure, function, and regulation within the vertebrate body, applying integrative and comparative approaches. Key organ systems, including the skin, skeleton, muscles, and nervous system, will be covered, while others—such as the respiratory, circulatory, reproductive, and endocrine systems—will be addressed in the following course, Human and Animal Physiology (HAP20306). The vertebrate phenotype is further contextualized within behavioral, ecological, and life-history strategies.  In the laboratory, students will explore vertebrate structure and function both macroscopically and microscopically. This includes a full anatomical exploration of a key vertebrate species with a special focus on the brain, along with histological analyses of vertebrate skin, muscles, and bones. In vivo physiological experiments will help illuminate how different systems integrate through sensor-integration-effector pathways. Several sessions will also incorporate digital learning tools for added support and insight.   NOTE: This course contains some practical work involving dissection. According to the Student Charter, based on conscientious objections, a dissection-free variant can be offered within this same course code. Registration for this variant is only possible by requesting this by email from the course coordinator prior to the course registration deadline. It requires consultation with, and approval from the course coordinator of this course.

texts.CO: In this course, the structure, development and physiology of plants is studied at the level of cells, tissues and the whole plant. The focus is on the form and function relationships with respect to the main functions of the plant. The course consists of a cell biological/structural part (with emphasis on cell structure and organisation, cell division, plant morphogenesis and differentiation) and a physiological part (focussing on e.g. photosynthesis, respiration, water and ion transport, regulation of growth by plant hormones and light, and interaction between plants and micro-organisms). Next to general principles also plant developmental flexibility gets attention, as well as the diversity in the plant kingdom, e.g. differences between monocots and dicots, plants with and without secondary growth, and plants with C3-, C4- or CAM-photosynthesis.  Aims of the course are the creation of a good knowledge of the relationship between structure and function of the various parts of the plant body, including processes that regulate growth and development of plants and their interrelationships. Students get experience in the methods used to investigate and analyse the structural and physiological phenomena involved.
texts.AC: The course consists of:  - lectures;  - practicals.  In the practical part physiological experiments will be performed and microscopical plant structure will be studied; this part also includes discussion sessions on the results of the practicals.

texts.CO: Biodiversity of the Netherlands provides an introduction to the plants and animals in the Netherlands, while focusing on the importance of biodiversity information and practical applications of this knowledge. The course consists of a botanical and zoological part of two weeks each. Students will learn how to identify higher plants and arthropods using diagnostic keys. Students will also be exposed to the diversity of mammals, birds and amphibians. They will also be expected to recognize a limited number of important taxa on sight. The identification of organisms will take place both during practicals and field excursions. To facilitate an understanding of biodiversity, assignments will be carried out both during practicals and field excursions. The field assignments will focus on making assessments and comparisons of plants and animals in certain areas and habitats. Students will gain knowledge about (woody) plant and arthropod morphology, nomenclature, classification, phylogenetic relationships, habitats, flora districts and the applicability of all of these to ecological studies. Students practise the recording of field observations and sample collection.
texts.AC: - attend the lectures;  - identify plants and arthropods during the practicals;  - perform individual assignments during the practicals;  - collect, study and identify plants and arthropods during the field excursions;  - perform group assignments during the field excursions and practicals. texts.CO: Physics, being a mathematical science, is being presented here as a tool to study biological phenomena. The emphasis is put on a handful of basic underlying principles and their use when trying to solve a diversity of problems from the realistic practice. The topics comprise basic optics (related to vision and microscopy),  the kinematics in one and two dimensions, dynamics, statics, hydrostatics and flow phenomena, kinetic theory of gases, thermal motion, diffusion, temperature and heat, calorimetry and phase changes, the steady state transfer of heat by conduction, convention and radiation.  Treating each of the above topics includes a descriptive survey of the basic physical concepts followed by a number of illustrative applications with a sufficient amount of biological details.

texts.CO: Sexual reproduction is one of the major characteristics of eukaryotes and involves a regular alternation between meiosis and fertilization. This course focuses on the basic principles of plant reproduction and the evolution of reproductive strategies in mosses, ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms. This knowledge is used as basis to understand the concepts that underlie sexual reproduction in dicot and monocot angiosperm species. Topics including flower induction, flower development, fertilization, embryogenesis, seed development and dispersal, and fruit-development are covered. This course aims to develop insight into evolutionary, regulatory and structural aspects of the reproductive strategies of plants. During the practicals experimental techniques used to obtain insight in structural aspects and developmental processes associated with plant reproduction are taught and practiced. These activities aim to prepare students to independently interpret reproductive strategies of any plant species.

texts.CO: Human and Animal Physiology is a 6 credits course that is closely related to the course Zoology (EZO10306 for BBI students and EZO10806 for BAS students) and continues on the functioning of organ systems. All these organ systems together are critical for all individual mammals to 1) function, 2) be able to maintain its internal environment (within certain limits), and 3) to adapt to the demands of the environment. The course is organized in themes, each theme dealing with metabolism and organ systems at the cellular, tissue and organismal level. The emphasis will be on the relationship between morphology, physiology and regulation of these organ systems. Each theme will be introduced during a lecture explaining the anatomy and physiology of the organ system involved and sometimes focused on certain specific details. The gained knowledge will then be practiced, repeated and deepened during the morphological, histological and physiological practicals. During a case study, the flexibility of the phenotype will be investigated, reported and presented in a poster, and discussed in an informal poster presentation. texts.AK: Modelling biological systems builds on first year biology courses, especially ecology, mathematics, statistics and physics. This basic knowledge is needed to adequately handle the models in the current course.
texts.CC: The following courses can be considered as a continuation of the learning outcomes of the present course: modelling in systems biology (SSB30806); key concepts in developmental biology (EZO22306); functional zoology (EZO30806); systems analysis and modelling (PPS20306); population and systems ecology (CSA20806); programming in Python (INF22306).
texts.CO: Biological systems are arguably the most complex systems science tries to understand. We make observations, and try to obtain useful insight in the systems. This requires hypotheses; ideas of how we believe the world around us is structured and operates. Models translate our hypotheses into concrete predictions about our objects of study that can be tested by targeted experiments.  The more complex the systems we study, the more crucial the use of models. The SARS-CoV2 outbreak is an example of a highly complex biological system. Models of how this virus spreads are crucial because they provide predictions that in turn can be used to take appropriate measures. Without models, we would not be able to focus the measures to combat this virus. There is a key role for one of the strongest tools in our scientific toolkit: mathematics. Mathematics are able to capture complexity in a form that makes it manageable. Mathematical models allow a full exploration of the consequences of our hypotheses and provide quantitative, and therefore precisely testable, predictions. Nowadays, this modelling toolkit is vastly extended by the wide availability of computers, which allow us to implement and test mathematical models, or even directly simulate the behaviour of complex systems.  In this course we attempt to convey the fascination for biological systems and introduce the tools to model them.

primaryContent.name: The Philosophy and Ethics of Biology

texts.AK: No prior knowledge assumed.
texts.CO: Biology as a science informs how we think of ourselves and of our relationship with nature. This course aims to understand the scientific character of contemporary biology, and how it gives influences problems in social ethics, animal ethics, environmental ethics, and the ethics of biotechnology.    There are two parts to the course:  1. Philosophy of science. How does biology explain phenomena, and how does that compare to other sciences (physics, anthropology)? How has this changed over time (from pre- to post-Darwinian biology)? What is the difference with religion, or with pseudo-science? How does biology progress and generate predictive theories? And finally, what are the values of biology as a science, and how is used to inform policy?   2. Ethics. We touch on the concept of "nature" and "human nature", and discuss how biology informs ethical discussions concerning human behavior, human-animal relations (speciesism, human uniqueness), environmental ethics (anthropocentrism, biocentrism), and biotech (genetic engineering, environmental engineering).

texts.CO: This course deals with the processes that coordinate the development of a single cell into a complex multi-cellular organism. In general, all cells of an organism originate from a single fertilized egg cell, and they share the same set of genes. However, they show differential gene expression and therefore, cells can have different functions within an organism. This course emphasises the molecular mechanisms by which differentiation is induced at the right place and time during development (=pattern formation) and on stem cells. Stem cells have the ability to develop into several -if not all- cell types (pluripotency). During the course, the similarities and differences in plant and animal developmental mechanisms are explained. Mechanisms that control pattern formation in plants as well as in animals are for example: - the formation of gradients of morphogens that are subsequently translated into distinct regions (tissues) with sharp borders; - cell communication leading to the induction of a new cell type at the interface; - noise that, by lateral inhibition, is translated into a pattern. The underlying molecular mechanisms of such developmental concepts will be explained during the course. For example, how does a morphogen gradient turn on key regulators in distinctive regions, which subsequently affect the expression of target genes, and how can small random differences between cells lead to a typical pattern formation by cell-cell communication?

texts.CO: Notes     This course is divided over two periods (5 & 6) and includes a field course. The course can only be completed in the correct order (first P5 then P6). Participation in the field course is not allowed without completing the program in Wageningen.    As postulated in the student charter a contribution must be paid to cover the cost of living during the field course.    In this course we study how have algae, fungi and invertebrate animals are adapted in structure, function, and behaviour to survive and reproduce in a wide spectrum of biotic and abiotic conditions. Next to that we also practice a set of skills that are important for the rest of your study (e.g. BSc-thesis) and your future career.  The questions about of Invertebrates, algae and fungi are discussed on phylogenetic and ontogenetic time scales. This provides insight in biodiversity, evolutionary theory and the social and economic importance of these groups. Following lectures, histological, dissection and other lab-exercises, all questions are finally integrated in a field course where invertebrate animals and algae are studied in their natural habitat of the intertidal zone (normally in Wimereux, France). There we can explore the adaptations and constraints of these highly diverse organisms, and their interactions in a natural community. You are also trained in doing research in a field work setting, and will practice some of the academic skills mentioned below.  Skills that will be incorporated in this course are all important for an doing research and can be seen as a preparation for the BSc-thesis and future careers. Participants will write a scientific paper about a research project performed in the same period. Participants will be trained in, and practice with, the use of information resources (library, internet sites, AI and portals) to optimize the writing. In addition students will get the chance to improve their papers based on feedback from reviewers as customary when submitting papers for publication. Students will practice communication skills by presenting their own findings to the rest of the group in different settings. During the field-course we will focus on skills for working in a scientific environment. Skills will include: maintaining a labjournal, feedback, teamwork, presenting, and writing skills.   NOTE: This course contains some practical work involving dissection. According to the Student Charter, based on conscientious objections, a dissection-free variant can be offered within this same course code. Registration for this variant is only possible by requesting this by email from the course coordinator prior to the course registration deadline. texts.CO: This course covers several more advanced statistical models and associated designs, and techniques for statistical inference, as relevant to life science studies. The main topics are categorical data, (multiple) regression, analysis of variance (including multiple comparisons), analysis of covariance, and non-parametric tests. The aims of an analysis, the model assumptions, the properties (and limitations) of the models and associated inferential techniques and the interpretation of results in terms of the practical problem will be discussed. Focus will be upon students gaining an understanding of the model ingredients, an (intuitive) understanding of inferential techniques, insight into data structures and implications for choice of model and analysis. Students will be able to perform analysis of data with statistical software, i.e. with R-Studio.

texts.CO: This introductory practical course provides basic knowledge and skills to study DNA, RNA, proteins and protein function. The majority of the course consists of laboratory practical. We work in 6 themes: DNA, RNA,  Recombinant DNA technology, proteins, 3D Structure & function and protein complexes.  Lectures provide the theoretical background on these themes and the techniques used during the lab practical are also discussed in theoretical e-learning modules. The practical are dedicated to analysis of DNA, RNA and proteins, both from prokaryotes (E. coli) and eukaryotes (tomato). They include isolation of DNA, RNA and proteins, construction of a physical map of a plasmid, cloning and detection techniques like PCR and western blotting. the study of protein function and enzyme kinetics, analysis of protein 3D structure using computer graphics and the discovery of cellular protein complexes with proteomics. Students will also learn basic skills for the use of computer programs and internet tools in the analysis of structure and function of DNA and proteins (bio-informatics). Rubisco will serve as a model in the majority of the experiments. At the end of the experiments students will report about their results and conclusions. The course is concluded with an theoretical exam.  The maximal capacity for this course is limited, both in periods 4 and 5. Students for which this course is compulsory or restricted optional will be admitted with priority.
